title: Commerce for Beginners
readerIntent: Understand eCommerce language, lifecycle, and Nodics ownership before reading the technical pages.
summary: A beginner-oriented explanation of how catalog, product, price, stock, cart, payment, delivery, order, and post-order operations work together without losing module ownership.

sections.heading: What is Commerce?
paragraphs: eCommerce is the business capability that lets an organization present products or services, price them, confirm availability, accept orders, take payment, deliver goods, and support post-order activity through digital channels.

A customer sees a simple journey: browse, add to cart, checkout, pay, receive, return if needed. A platform sees many separate business authorities working together: catalog, product, price, inventory, cart, payment, fulfillment, order, communication, audit, and reporting.

sections.heading: The simple customer journey
items: Discover: a website, app, marketplace, or API presents content and products.
Evaluate: product information, images, price, availability, taxes, promotions, and delivery promises help the customer decide.
Commit intent: the customer adds one or more items to a cart.
Checkout: the customer chooses address, delivery option, payment method, and confirms the purchase.
Place order: the platform validates the final cart, creates an order, commits governed stock/payment evidence, and starts fulfillment.
Fulfill: warehouse, pickup, digital delivery, carrier, or partner processes complete delivery.
Operate after sale: cancellation, return, refund, invoice, notification, reconciliation, and customer service use the recorded evidence.

sections.heading: How Nodics separates responsibility
items: Product describes what is being sold. It does not decide price, stock, delivery, or payment.
Pricing decides monetary value in context. It does not edit product identity or stock balances.
Inventory decides stock, reservations, allocations, warehouses, pools, sourcing, pre-order, backorder, and overbooking policy.
Cart records pre-order customer intent and can change while the customer is shopping.
Order records the final commercial projection created from checkout. It should be stable enough for audit, fulfillment, payment, and customer service.
Payment owns payment methods, provider adapters, authorization/capture/refund evidence, retries, and reconciliation.
Fulfillment owns delivery modes, carrier/provider adapters, consignments, shipments, labels, tracking, returns, and warehouse handoff evidence.
CMS and Storefront own the customer presentation context and website resolution, not the authoritative commerce data.

sections.heading: Why this matters for customization
paragraphs: Enterprise projects rarely use exactly one payment gateway, one warehouse, one shipping provider, one tax rule, or one catalog structure. Nodics keeps capabilities modular so customers can add a new module layer with extra schema fields, validation, provider adapters, policies, Axis metadata, and documentation without changing the framework module.

The safest customization rule is: extend the owning module or add a later customer module that composes it. Do not duplicate the same business state in Axis, Storefront, or another module just because the UI needs to display it.

sections.heading: Beginner glossary
items: Catalog: a governed collection of products or content used for authoring and delivery.
Product: the business identity of an item or service.
Variant: a sellable variation such as size, color, storage, or configuration.
Price: the resolved monetary amount for a product in a context such as currency, customer, channel, date, or quantity.
Stock: inventory quantity controlled by warehouse, pool, unit, and policy.
Cart entry: an item in a cart, usually product plus quantity and selected options.
Order entry: the final order-side copy of the commercial line after placement.
Delivery group: a checkout grouping such as ship-to-address, pickup, digital delivery, or scheduled delivery.
Payment group: a checkout grouping such as card payment, wallet, cash on delivery, advance, or offline payment.
Allocation: a quantity-level relationship that says which part of a line belongs to which delivery, payment, reservation, or fulfillment evidence.
Provider: an external or internal implementation such as Stripe, PayPal, CyberSource, DHL, FedEx, Aramex, a warehouse system, or a custom ERP connector.
Policy: backend-governed rules that decide whether a method, provider, stock behavior, or action is allowed.
